title: Area V review: Performance Maneuvers and Ground Reference Maneuvers
intro: These questions mix both Tasks of Area V: steep turns and ground reference maneuvers. Many join the two, because the same load factor, stall speed and wind ideas show up in both.

questions.q: You plan ground reference maneuvers over farmland where the ground is 1,200 feet MSL. Which altimeter reading puts you in the ACS altitude range for this Task?
options: 1,600 feet MSL
2,000 feet MSL
2,400 feet MSL
3,200 feet MSL
questions.why: The range is 600 to 1,000 feet AGL, so 1,800 to 2,200 feet MSL here (ACS PA.V.B.S3). 2,000 feet MSL is 800 feet AGL [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. 1,600 MSL is only 400 AGL, and 2,400 MSL is 1,200 AGL.

questions.q: Your POH says the airplane stalls at 60 knots with the wings level. About what is the stall speed in a level, coordinated 45° steep turn?
options: 60 knots
About 71 knots
About 85 knots
120 knots
questions.why: A level 45° turn gives a load factor of 1.41, and stall speed rises with the square root of load factor. The square root of 1.41 is about 1.19, and 60 × 1.19 ≈ 71 knots. The AFH example is the same idea: 50 knots wings level becomes 60 knots at 45° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

questions.q: In a turn around a point, why do you need your steepest bank on the downwind side?
options: Groundspeed is highest there, so you have less time to turn, and more bank gives a faster rate of turn
Airspeed is highest there, so the airplane can handle more bank
The tailwind tries to roll the wings level, so you must bank more to fight it
Load factor is lowest on the downwind side, so a steep bank costs nothing
questions.why: At high groundspeed there is less time to turn, so you bank more to raise the rate of turn [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. At a given airspeed, more bank means a faster rate of turn [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. Your airspeed stays the same all the way around; only groundspeed changes.

questions.q: You enter a steep turn on a heading of 090° at 3,500 feet and 95 knots. Which result is within all the private pilot ACS standards?
options: Rolled out on 090°, airspeed 107 knots, altitude 3,450 feet
Rolled out on 078°, airspeed 95 knots, altitude 3,500 feet
Rolled out on 098°, airspeed 103 knots, altitude 3,560 feet
Rolled out on 090°, airspeed 95 knots, altitude 3,620 feet
questions.why: The standards are entry altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, and rollout on the entry heading ±10° (ACS PA.V.A.S5). 107 knots is 12 knots fast, 078° is 12° off, and 3,620 feet is 120 feet high. Time the rollout so the wings are level on the entry heading [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

questions.q: You fly along a road with a 20-knot wind blowing from 45° off your right nose. If you do not correct, about how fast does the wind push you sideways?
options: About 7 knots
About 10 knots
A little over 14 knots
20 knots
questions.why: A wind halfway between the nose and the side causes sideways drift of up to just over 70 percent of the wind speed. 0.7 × 20 = 14, so a little over 14 knots [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. Only a wind straight from the side drifts you at the full 20 knots.

questions.q: During turns around a point, your steepest bank, on the downwind side, is 45°. You are holding altitude. What is true at that moment?
options: The load factor is about 1.41 G, so your stall speed is higher than with the wings level
The load factor is 1 G, because you are holding altitude
The load factor is lower than in still air, because the tailwind adds groundspeed
The load factor is 2 G, so your stall speed doubles
questions.why: Any airplane in a level 45° turn has a load factor of 1.41, no matter its speed, and stall speed goes up with the square root of load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. This is why the AFH says to avoid banks over 45° in ground reference maneuvers [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

questions.q: You fly a rectangular course. The wind is on your tail on the downwind leg. Which turn needs the shallowest bank?
options: Downwind leg to base leg
Base leg to upwind leg
Crosswind leg to downwind leg
Upwind leg to crosswind leg
questions.why: Coming off the upwind leg you have a headwind and your lowest groundspeed, so you roll slowly into a shallow bank. Downwind to base is steep, and base to upwind and crosswind to downwind are medium [[24:152|AFH 7-6]].

questions.q: In a 30° turn you relax the aileron to neutral, and the bank stays where it is. Later, in a 50° steep turn, you do the same. What happens?
options: The bank stays at 50°, just like the 30° turn
The bank keeps getting steeper unless you hold opposite aileron
The wings slowly roll back toward level by themselves
The nose pitches up and the airplane climbs
questions.why: Medium banks, about 20° to 45°, tend to stay put with neutral aileron. At about 45° or more, the airplane keeps rolling into the bank unless you hold opposite aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. The faster outside wing makes more lift [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

questions.q: You roll into a turn around a point on the downwind side and find you need about 55° of bank to hold your circle. What does the AFH say to do?
options: Exit the maneuver and set up again farther from the point
Keep the 55° bank, since it is under the 60° parachute limit
Shallow to 30° and add inside rudder to keep the nose coming around
Keep the bank and pull harder to tighten the circle
questions.why: If the bank is too steep, exit right away and move farther from the reference. Avoid banks over 45° because stall speed goes up [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Inside rudder to hurry the turn is a skid, which can lead to a cross-control stall and spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: You fly a 45° bank turn at 90 knots true airspeed. The tangent of 45° is 1. Using the PHAK rate of turn formula, about how fast do you turn, and how long does a full circle take?
options: About 6° per second, so about 60 seconds for 360°
About 3° per second, so about 2 minutes for 360°
About 12° per second, so about 30 seconds for 360°
About 24° per second, so about 15 seconds for 360°
questions.why: Rate of turn = 1,091 × tan(bank) ÷ airspeed in knots [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. 1,091 × 1 ÷ 90 ≈ 12.1° per second, and 360 ÷ 12.1 ≈ 30 seconds [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. That steep bank is why a steep turn makes a quick, tight circle.

questions.q: You fly turns around a point at 85 knots airspeed in a 15-knot wind. About what is your groundspeed headed straight downwind, and headed straight upwind?
options: 100 knots downwind, 70 knots upwind
85 knots both ways, since airspeed stays the same
70 knots downwind, 100 knots upwind
100 knots downwind, 85 knots upwind
questions.why: Headed downwind, the tailwind adds to your airspeed: 85 + 15 = 100 knots. Headed upwind, the headwind subtracts: 85 - 15 = 70 knots [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. The AFH example works the same way: 90 knots plus a 10-knot tailwind is 100 knots groundspeed [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

questions.q: Today you fly steep turns, then turns around a point, solo with half fuel. The POH gives a maneuvering speed (VA) of 105 knots at maximum gross weight. Which plan is best?
options: Fly at 105 knots, because that is the published VA
Fly up to about 115 knots, because a lighter airplane can handle more speed
Use any speed in the green arc, because VA only matters in turbulence
Fly slower than 105 knots, because VA goes down as weight goes down
questions.why: VA depends on weight: it may be 100 knots when heavy but only 90 knots when light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Fly steep turns at or below VA [[24:211|AFH 10-2]], and ground reference maneuvers no faster than maneuvering speed [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. A light airplane has a lower VA than the max-weight number.

questions.q: You are on the upwind half of a turn around a point, with a headwind or quartering headwind. Where should the airplane's nose point compared with the circle you are tracking?
options: Angled toward the inside of the circle
Angled toward the outside of the circle
Straight at the point in the middle
Exactly along the circle, with no correction
questions.why: During the downwind half, adjust the heading toward the inside of the turn. During the upwind half, adjust it toward the outside [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

questions.q: A trainer at 90 knots and a faster airplane at 150 knots each fly a level, coordinated 60° bank turn. How do their load factors compare?
options: The faster airplane has more load factor
The slower airplane has more load factor
Both are 1.41 G
They are the same: 2 G for both
questions.why: For a given bank in a level turn, every airplane gets the same load factor, no matter the airspeed. At 60° it is 2.0, so the effective weight doubles [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Speed changes the rate and radius of the turn, not the load factor.

questions.q: A student flies the rectangular course only a few hundred feet outside the field edges. What is the main problem?
options: The legs become too long to hold altitude
The wind can no longer cause drift so close to the field
The turns need very steep banks, which raise the load factor and the stall speed
There is no problem; closer is more precise
questions.why: Fly ½ to ¾ mile from the field edges. Flying close to the references forces very steep banks, raising load factor and stall speed [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. A level 60° bank already doubles the load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

questions.q: You start a 45° steep turn to the right on a heading of 030°. About what heading should you start rolling out to finish on 030°?
options: About 052°
About 345°
About 008°
questions.why: Start the rollout at half the bank angle before the entry heading [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Half of 45° is about 22°. In a right turn the heading counts up toward 030°, so start near 030 - 22 = 008°.

questions.q: Flying along a road at 100 knots with a 10-knot direct crosswind, you need about 6° of wind correction. You slow to 80 knots, and the wind stays the same. What happens to the wind correction angle you need?
options: It gets smaller
It gets larger
It stays the same, since the wind did not change
It drops to zero
questions.why: At 100 knots, a 10-knot direct crosswind needs about 6° [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Like a boat crossing a river, a slower forward speed or a faster current needs a bigger angle into the flow [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

questions.q: In a steep turn you pull too hard. The stall warning sounds and you feel a buffet. The turn is coordinated. What should you do first?
options: Ease forward on the elevator to lower the angle of attack, then level the wings, coordinate, and adjust power
Pull back harder to hold altitude
Add full power and keep the same bank and back pressure
Press hard inside rudder to bring the nose up
questions.why: A stall above 1 G, as in a steep turn, is an accelerated stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Recover by applying forward elevator to reduce the angle of attack, level the wings with ailerons, coordinate with rudder, and adjust power. Waiting can lead to a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: When should your wings be level during S-turns across a road?
options: At the 90° crosswind point of each half-circle
For a few seconds after crossing the road, to check the wind
Just as you cross the road, then roll right into the turn the other way
Only at the end of the whole maneuver
questions.why: Time the rollout so the wings become level just as you cross the road, then start the opposite turn with no delay [[24:156|AFH 7-10]]. At the 90° point you are crosswind and holding a crab, not wings level [[24:155|AFH 7-9]].

questions.q: You roll into a 45° steep turn. Generally, by about what bank should you start adding back pressure and power?
options: Before about 10° of bank
Once you reach 45° of bank
Only after the altimeter shows a loss
Before about 30° of bank
questions.why: As the bank is set up, generally before 30°, smoothly add back pressure to raise the angle of attack, and add power to hold airspeed against the extra drag [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

questions.q: Why is scanning for traffic extra important while you fly ground reference maneuvers?
options: Other pilots must give way to an airplane doing training maneuvers
Over a quarter of fatal accidents happen in maneuvering flight, and the maneuver pulls your attention away from scanning
Other aircraft are not allowed below 1,000 feet AGL, so any you see are breaking the rules
Your airplane's wings block your view only during these maneuvers
questions.why: More than a quarter (26.6 percent) of fatal accidents in 10 years happened in maneuvering flight, and the distraction of the maneuver takes away from scanning for traffic [[16:12|AC 90-48E 11.2.2.1]]. Also look for helicopters, towers and wires [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Every pilot must see and avoid other aircraft; no one has to give way to you because you are practicing [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

questions.q: A student keeps gaining and losing altitude in steep turns. They watch only the nose. What does the AFH suggest?
options: Keep eyes on the altimeter and fly by the instruments
Look only at the ball to keep the turn coordinated
Watch both the nose and the wings against the horizon
Pick a closer reference point on the ground
questions.why: A pilot who watches only the nose will have trouble holding altitude. One who watches both the nose and the wings against the horizon can likely stay within standards [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Flying by the instruments instead of outside references is a common error [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
